newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senate panel plans Superfund bill vote Sep 11.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senate panel plans Superfund bill vote Sep 11.

text.p: The U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee plans to vote September 11 on a bill to overhaul the multibillion dollar Superfund toxic waste cleanup program, senate aides said Tuesday.
The committee plans to hold a hearing September 4 on the long-awaited proposal after circulating a draft next week, industry and environmental lobbyists said.

Details of the bill were being closely held, and it was unclear whether issues that have long been sticking points in the debate over improving the Superfund program -- such as who should pay cleanup costs -- had been resolved.

While lobbyists said Republicans and Democrats had given up on negotiating a bipartisan proposal, an aide to Sen. John Chafee, chairman of the committee, said the two sides were "definitely still talking."

Industrial companies and their insurers have pushed to make the government pay all the cleanup costs at sites where companies dumped waste legally before 1980. But the Clinton administration has stood firm on holding big companies responsible for cleaning up pollution they caused.
Debate over the last 18 months has centered on defining who should be exempt from paying cleanup costs.

Lawmakers and the administration have proposed to let local communities off the hook for paying to decontaminate landfills where they dumped garbage, leaving cleanup costs at those sites in the hands of the government and companies that dumped toxic waste there.
"Any bill that reduces the number of (liable) parties and lawyers ... we think that's significant reform. We'd support it," said Dan Zielinski, spokesman for the American Insurance Association.
The key question at municipal landfills will be who should cover the costs of getting rid of pollution that was dumped by companies that are now defunct or cannot be identified.
Under the existing Superfund program, those costs are shared by the remaining identifiable responsible parties.
Other key issues that the bill will have to address are cleanup standards and penalties for damaging the environment.
